questions.learningObjective: diagnose a write through a list whose wildcard extends a bound
questions.stem: A client writes List<? extends Number> xs = new ArrayList<Integer>(); xs.add(4); and prints xs. What does the compiler report?

options.text: incompatible types, because int cannot be converted to CAP#1, the capture of ? extends Number
the method add cannot be applied, because the list holds an unknown subtype of Number
options.misconception: the add is refused because the element type is an unknown capture

options.text: int cannot be converted to Number, so the value does not fit the parameter
options.misconception: an Integer is not a Number and so the value is rejected

options.text: the wildcard makes the list unmodifiable, so add is refused
options.misconception: a wildcard parameter turns the list into an unmodifiable one

questions.explanation: An extends bound lets the method read elements, since every one is a Number, but it promises nothing about which subtype is actually there, so there is no argument type the compiler can guarantee is safe to add, and it reports the capture type instead. The tempting answers each name a rule that is not this one: the bound never makes a list unmodifiable, an Integer is a Number, and the failure is about the add, not about reading.
questions.hint: Ask what the extends bound says about adding rather than about reading.

questions.learningObjective: trace a write through a list whose wildcard has a super bound
questions.stem: A method is declared static void fill(List<? super Integer> sink, int v) and its body is sink.add(v). A client passes a List<Object>, then prints the list and the simple name of the runtime type of its first element. What is printed?

the list prints as [9] and the element reports Object

options.misconception: a super wildcard refuses writes and leaves the list empty

questions.learningObjective: diagnose two overloads that erase to the same signature
questions.stem: A class declares static boolean same(List<String> a, List<String> b) and static boolean same(List<Integer> a, List<Integer> b), both comparing their arguments. The developer reports the compiler refuses the class. What is the fault?

options.text: Both methods have the same erasure once the type arguments are removed
the two signatures are textually identical, so the second is a duplicate
options.misconception: the erasure makes the two written signatures identical

options.text: a generic method may not be overloaded on its type arguments at all
options.misconception: overloading on type arguments is forbidden for any method

options.text: the compiler keeps the more specific type argument and drops the other
options.misconception: the compiler picks the overload with the more specific argument

n.intValue()

questions.stem: class Outer holds a private int secret, an inner class Peek with its own private int first, a make method that returns a new Peek, and a read method that takes a Peek and returns its first field. A client builds an Outer, makes a Peek, sets secret to 42, then prints p.cached(), p.now() and o.read(p). What is printed?

options.misconception: the cached copy and the live read both show the new value
the outer setter cannot reach the field the inner class reads
the outer class cannot read a private field of its inner class

A client opens two tallies from one bag, calls add twice on the first and once on the second, then prints t.show(), u.show() and b.peek(t). What is printed?

the second tally carries a private item count of its own
the two counters swap places between the tallies

questions.learningObjective: trace a static list that keeps enclosing objects alive
questions.stem: class Session { private final String user; private int events = 0; Session(String user) { this.user = user; } class Recorder { void mark() { events = events + 1; } int events() { return events; } String who() { return user; } } static final List<Recorder> LIVE = new ArrayList<Recorder>(); static Session open(String user) { Session s = new Session(user); s.attach(); return s; } Recorder attach() { Recorder r = new Recorder(); LIVE.add(r); return r; } } Session.open("ada"); Session.open("bo"); Session.LIVE.get(0).mark(); Session.LIVE.get(0).mark(); Session.LIVE.get(1).mark(); System.out.println(Session.LIVE.get(0).events() + " " + Session.LIVE.get(0).who()); System.out.println(Session.LIVE.get(1).events() + " " + Session.LIVE.get(1).who()); What is printed?

options.text: 2 ada on the first line, then 1 bo on the second
1 ada on the first line, then 1 bo on the second
options.misconception: the two marks on the first recorder collapse into one event

options.text: 2 ada on the first line, then 1 bo, both counted for one session
options.misconception: the static list is shared, so every recorder reports the same count

options.text: nothing at all, because the sessions are no longer reachable
options.misconception: dropping a session reference also drops its inner object

questions.explanation: Each recorder holds a reference to the session that built it, so a recorder in a static list keeps that session alive even after every local name for it has gone, and its mark still writes into the session's own counter. The tempting answers each assume a loss of reachability that never happens: nothing collapses the counts, the two sessions are separate objects, and dropping a local reference does not drop an object something else still points at.
questions.hint: Ask which object the recorder in the list still points at.

questions.stem: class Watch holds a private level and a private seen. Its inner class Probe has a constructor that copies level into its own field, accessors cached() and live(), and methods attach() returning a new Probe and raise() that adds one to level. A client attaches a probe, raises twice, and prints cached(), live() and the outer's seen. The program prints 1/3/1. What is the fault?

options.text: The probe copies level in its constructor, so cached can never see a later change
raise adds to level, but the outer's seen field shadows it
options.misconception: the outer's seen field shadows the level the probe reads

options.text: The cached accessor reads the outer's field, which is the wrong object
options.misconception: cached reads the outer's live field instead of its own copy

options.text: attach builds the probe before level has its first value
options.misconception: the probe is created too early, before level is set

The tempting answers each misidentify which value is stale: the outer field is being updated correctly, the cached accessor is faithfully returning its own copy, and the probe is built after level already holds 1.
questions.hint: Ask whether the probe's accessor reads the outer field or its own field.

each bump starts from zero regardless of the earlier calls
the static list keeps only the most recently parked bump

questions.stem: class Base has a final int total() returning part() + 1 and a protected int part() returning 10, and class Sub overrides part() to return 20. A client holds the subclass in a Base variable and prints total() and part(). What is printed?

options.misconception: the override is ignored because the variable is typed as the base type
the final method bypasses the override and calls the base hook
the final method hands back only the hook's value

questions.explanation: total is final so the subclass cannot replace it, but the part call inside it still dispatches on the runtime type, so the overridden 20 is what gets added to 1 and the same 20 comes back from a direct call. questions.learningObjective: diagnose a subclass that tries to replace a final method
questions.stem: class Base has a final int total() and class Sub declares public int total() returning 999. A client calls total() on a Sub held in a Base variable. The developer reports the compiler refuses the program. What is the fault?

options.text: Sub declares an override of a method the parent marked final
the final method total in Base is not visible inside Sub
options.misconception: a final method is hidden from the subclass

options.text: Sub must be declared final because its parent has a final method
options.misconception: the subclass needs the final keyword to override anything

options.text: the program is legal, and the subclass version is used at run time
options.misconception: a later declaration silently wins over a final one

questions.explanation: A final method is exactly the way a class refuses to let a subclass replace one of its steps, so the compiler stops the override before the program can run. The tempting answers each pick a different excuse: final does not hide a method, the subclass needs no modifier of its own, and there is no run-time tie-break, because the conflict is caught as an error rather than resolved at run time.
questions.hint: Ask what the final modifier on the parent's method forbids.

report reads a value that has not been written yet
options.misconception: report runs before the last call has finished writing

options.misconception: the override delegates upward, so nothing is skipped

static void record(int v)

questions.stem: class Base2 declares a private int report() and a package-private void hook() that both print the private field, and class Sub2 extends Base2 overriding hook() to call report() twice over. A client calls both methods on the subclass. What does the compiler report?

options.text: cannot find symbol for report(), because a private method is not inherited
cannot find symbol for report(), because the field report reads is private
options.misconception: privacy of the field inside report is what the subclass trips on

options.misconception: a private method of the superclass is callable from any subclass

options.misconception: a package-private method is hidden from a subclass in the same package
